Aiken County by the numbers

Where is Aiken County and what is in it?

Aiken County is in western South Carolina, across the Savannah River from Georgia, and is part of the Augusta-Richmond County metropolitan area. It covers 1,080.17 square miles, which makes it the fourth-largest South Carolina county by land area.

The county seat and largest community is the city of Aiken. Other cities are New Ellenton and North Augusta, which is partly in Edgefield County. The towns are Burnettown, Jackson, Perry, Salley, Monetta, Wagener and Windsor, and census-designated places include Beech Island, Graniteville, Clearwater and Warrenville.

The land runs from the Piedmont in the north through the Sandhills to the Coastal Plain in the south. It borders Saluda, Lexington, Orangeburg, Barnwell and Edgefield counties, plus Burke and Richmond counties in Georgia. A seller in a town such as Wagener faces a different market than one in North Augusta, even though both mail their tax payment to the same county.

What is the history that shapes Aiken County today?

Aiken County was organized in 1871 from parts of Barnwell, Edgefield, Lexington and Orangeburg counties. It was named for William Aiken, the first president of the South Carolina Railroad Company.

Two later events changed the map. In the late 19th century the county became a winter refuge for wealthy Northerners, who built large houses, and it remains known for horse training because the winters are mild. In the 1950s the Savannah River Site was built, which required acquiring the town of Ellenton. Its residents and businesses moved about eight miles north to New Ellenton and about five miles south to Jackson.

The county grew from 53,137 residents in 1950 to 81,038 in 1960, then reached 168,808 in 2020. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 181,515.

When are Aiken County property taxes due?

South Carolina law makes property tax payable between September 30 and January 15 after the assessment. The county treasurer collects under the Department of Revenue's supervision, and receipts must describe real estate by tax map number.

Under the penalty statute, a bill unpaid before January 16, or 30 days after the notice is mailed if that is later, picks up a 3% penalty. A further 7% is added if it remains unpaid before February 2, and another 5% before March 17. After March 17 the treasurer issues an execution to the delinquent collector. A U.S. postmark is the determining date for mailed payments.

These come from a Justia copy of the state code, which carries a notice that it may not be the latest version. The Aiken County Treasurer can confirm the amounts on your bill, and we could not open the county's treasurer page, so we do not list its hours or address.

What happens to penalties when a house changes hands?

If the title to real property moves during a tax year and the county mailed the notice to the prior owner, the treasurer shall waive the penalty when the new owner got no timely notice. This is in subsection (B) of the penalty statute.
